To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the genetic basis of EA is more sensitive to population differentiation than height, and that the genetic basis for height and EA is sensitive to the effect of latitude on selection pressures.

(1) polygenic scores (PGs) of height and educational attainment are significantly correlated with population averages of these traits (r ~0,9); (2) polygenic scores of educational attainment are moderately correlated with latitude (r= 67); (3) the effect of latitude on polygenic scores for educational attainment is reduced but remains significant after adding the variable of sub continental group; (4) global Fst index reveals population differentiation at height, educational attainment, and random SNPs

1) polygenic scores for educational attainment and height are significantly correlated with average IQ and height in ethnic groups, 2) polygenic scores differ across populations, 3) the correlation between population differences and latitude is reduced when controlling for continental groups, and 4) polygenic scores are more sensitive to selection than Fst, and are more robust to linkage disequilibrium decay than Fst.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of selection on polygenic traits.
two highly polygenic phenotypes that have been under directional selection in the human species: height and EA.
selection on polygenic traits in humans, and the genetic and demographic factors influencing population differentiation in polygenic scores.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

selection for EA and height has been stronger on Europeans and East Asians compared to sub-Saharan Africans, but the differences in selection pressure across groups are not as large as the PGS differences.
the genetic basis of EA is under stronger directional selection than height and that this selection has a global impact, but is not uniform across ethnicities.
the PGS differences are a more robust and informative measure of selection than Fst, and they are also more sensitive to the effect of LD decay and the significance of GWAs loci.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is strong evidence of selection on EA and height.
there is evidence for divergent selection on height, but the evidence for cognitive ability is weaker.
selection on height and EA is stronger in populations with lower latitude.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic architecture of EA and height is consistent with divergent selection pressures, with the effect of selection being stronger on EA.
polygenic scores are more sensitive to population differentiation than the Fst index.

the PGS of EA and height show a remarkable correlation with the average IQ and stature of ethnic groups, and that the effect of latitude on EA PGS was reduced but remained significant when the effect of continental groups was accounted for.
